fatal_errors: The proposed protective-oxide mechanism is not supported by either cited source and omits the target lattice-disorder/dislocation mechanism.
The predicted improvement in wear resistance at elevated temperature is opposite to the sharp deterioration above approximately 900 K in the target.
The reciprocating 10–100 N test conditions do not reconstruct the nanoscale indentation/friction intervention or its loading boundaries.
The experiment measures wear and friction but does not measure oxide formation, so it cannot establish the proposed mediator.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad application—high-temperature wear of an FeNiCrCoCu coating—and uses room temperature as a baseline, but otherwise has little agreement with the target. The target predicts stable hardness and wear resistance through 600 K, followed by lattice disorder, dislocation-density changes, softening, and increased, fluctuating friction at 900–1200 K. The generated hypothesis instead invokes protective oxidation and predicts improved wear resistance. Its temperature and macroscopic load ranges are arbitrary relative to the specified nanoscale simulation. E1 concerns a different precipitate-strengthened high-entropy alloy under tensile creep, while E2 gives general HEA background; neither supports protective oxide formation or tribological improvement in FeNiCrCoCu. Although the falsification rule is quantitative, the experiment lacks oxide characterization and therefore cannot discriminate oxide-mediated protection from unrelated thermal effects.
